title: Attitudes to Democracy, Information Sources, and Self-Reported Misinformation Exposure in a Federal Election: An Australian Experience Sampling Study
screen_reason: Five-day experience sampling study (four surveys/day) around the 2025 Australian Federal Election, N = 123 Australian residents, 2,278 ESM observations. Each ESM survey asked 'since the last survey, have you seen or heard misinformation about the Australian election?' (Yes/No). The paper reports the share of participants who reported any misinformation exposure (50.41%), the share of surveys in which misinformation was reported (17.72%), and the mean number of instances per participant (2.37). These are self-reported exposure shares with stated denominators, so RECALL (subtype exposure).

estimates.date: Five days surrounding the 2025 Australian Federal Election (two days before, election day, two days after), 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of participants who reported seeing election-related misinformation at least once during the five-day experience sampling period
estimates.denominator: 123 participants residing in Australia for the duration of the election, retained after pre-registered exclusions
estimates.definition: Answered 'Yes' at least once across the ESM period to 'since the last survey, have you seen or heard misinformation about the Australian election?'
estimates.misinfo_def: No external definition applied; the item asks about "what they thought was misinformation related to the Australian election", i.e. respondent-defined
estimates.source_quote: Addressing RQ1, within our sample, 50.41% of participants (n = 62) reported seeing election-related misinformation during the 5-days surrounding the election.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Participant self-report; no external veracity check of what was seen. Momentary yes/no item delivered via the SEMA3 app; mean compliance 67.24% (SD = 27.01).
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were a convenience sample recruited via a first-year psychology research participation pool in exchange for course credit (n = 5), on-campus and social media advertising to go in the draw for a $50 gift card (n = 58), and the crowdsourcing platform Prolific.
estimates.notes: denom_scope=population per the survey rule. breadth coded 'misleading' as the loosest veracity band because the numerator is respondent-defined with no external standard; arguably it should be blank.

estimates.measure_type: % of completed experience sampling surveys in which the participant reported seeing or hearing election misinformation since the previous survey
estimates.denominator: 2,278 completed experience sampling observations from 123 participants (four surveys per day for five days)

estimates.moderator_quote: We also calculated descriptive statistics for frequency variables (e.g., information use, misinformation exposure, political polarisation exposure) in the experience sampling period through average percentages relative to surveys completed.
estimates.notes: A momentary rather than person-level share: the denominator is survey occasions, not people, so it is not a duplicate of the 50.41% row. The paper describes it as an average percentage relative to surveys completed, which may be a mean of within-person percentages rather than a pooled observation-level share; the text does not disambiguate. unit='exposure' used for the survey-occasion denominator; the schema has no 'observation' value.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) baseline and follow-up misinformation-frequency means ('an average frequency of 3.28 times' at baseline, '2.32 times' at follow-up). These are means on the 9-point Never-to-Hourly-or-more scale, not shares of respondents, so the instructions exclude them; the text reads as if they were counts of times, but the Measures section defines the item as a 9-point frequency scale, which is an inconsistency worth a human's eye. (b) Source attribution for misinformation exposure is reported only as an ordering (social media, then conversation, then commercial TV news and 'Other') with mean counts shown in Figure 1; no per-platform share with a denominator is stated in the text, so no platform-split rows could be made. The figure itself is not in the text file. (c) 61.79% of participants reporting a politically divisive situation, and 19.15% of surveys - political division, not misinformation. (d) All multilevel model coefficients (misinformation exposure predicting trust, democracy attitudes, polarisation) are effects, not prevalence.

rob.design: Pre-registered experience sampling study around the 2025 Australian Federal Election. Convenience sample recruited from a first-year psychology pool (n = 5), on-campus and social media advertising (n = 58) and Prolific (n = 60); 123 retained after pre-registered exclusions (no baseline survey n = 2, no ESM surveys n = 4, two failed attention checks n = 2, non-Australian timezone n = 2). Mean age 34.5 (SD 12.1); 66 women, 54 men, 3 non-binary/prefer not to say; sample left-leaning (M = 32.8 on a 0-100 left-right slider); 95.1% eligible to vote. Design: baseline survey in the week before the election, then four SEMA3 app surveys per day for five days (pseudorandom 90-minute windows 09:00-19:30, 60-minute response window, minimum 30 minutes between surveys), then a follow-up two weeks after the result. 2,278 ESM observations (1,301 before or on election day, 977 after); mean compliance 67.24% (SD 27.01); careless responses under 650 ms removed (<0.22% of items); eight surveys removed for spacing. Exposure measured entirely by self-report with no external verification, so the estimates index perceived rather than verified misinformation.
rob.item6_quote: Participants were then asked ‘since the last survey, have you seen or heard misinformation about the Australian election?’ (Yes/No). If participants answered yes, they were asked to indicate where they had seen or heard misinformation about the Australian election, with the same source options as information use.
rob.item10_quote: Addressing RQ1, within our sample, 50.41% of participants (n = 62) reported seeing election-related misinformation during the 5-days surrounding the election. On average, participants reported 2.37 instances of misinformation across the ESM period, and in 17.72% of surveys answered.
